title: Autonomous Navigation: All of It Together
description: Every sense in this course, combined into one loop: map the world, know where you are in it, plan a path, drive — and replan the instant something changes.

content.value: This is the module's final destination: a robot that can cross a room it's never seen, using nothing but its own senses. It's built from five stages, running continuously — not once, but again and again, because the world doesn't hold still.

content.title: 🗺️ Walk through autonomous navigation
content.hint: This is the whole course, one more time, at its most capable.

stages.label: Map
stages.detail: Build a picture of the surroundings — Module 8's LiDAR point cloud, or a series of ultrasonic pings, turned into a map of walls and open space.

stages.label: Localise
stages.detail: Work out where the robot itself sits within that map. Without this step, a perfect map is useless — you need to know your own position on it.

stages.label: Plan
stages.detail: Given the map and the robot's position, calculate a path from here to the goal that avoids every known obstacle.

stages.label: Drive
stages.detail: Follow that planned path using differential drive, exactly as Module 5 taught — two wheel speeds, nothing more.

stages.label: Replan
stages.detail: A new obstacle appears that wasn't on the original map. Rather than crashing into it, the robot updates its map and recalculates a path around it, live.

content.value: Why Replanning Is the Real Test

Any robot can follow a fixed path through an empty, known room. The genuinely hard, genuinely valuable part is stage five: something changes — a door closes, someone walks through, a box gets left on the floor — and the robot notices and adapts, instead of blindly continuing a plan that's no longer valid.

Notice this entire five-stage loop is still, underneath everything, sense (map, localise), think (plan), act (drive), repeat (replan) — Module 1's loop, run at a scale that took this whole course to build up to.

You've now met every idea autonomous navigation depends on: sensors from Modules 7-8, movement from Module 5, and decision-making from Module 9-10. Nothing about this lesson is new physics — it's everything you already know, composed into one system.

Key takeaway: autonomous navigation is map, localise, plan, drive and replan, running continuously. Replanning when the world changes — not just following a fixed plan — is what makes a robot genuinely autonomous rather than merely automatic.

quiz.question: Why is 'localise' a separate stage from 'map'?
options: It isn't really separate, they're the same step
A perfect map is useless without also knowing where the robot itself currently sits within it
Localising happens before any sensors are used at all
quiz.explain: Knowing the world's layout and knowing your own position in it are genuinely two different problems, both needed to plan a path.

quiz.question: What makes the 'replan' stage the real test of an autonomous system, rather than just a nice extra?
options: It's optional and rarely used in practice
It's what lets the robot adapt when the world doesn't match its original map, instead of blindly following an outdated plan
It only matters for very large rooms
quiz.explain: A fixed plan through a known, unchanging room is the easy case. Genuine autonomy shows up when something unexpected happens and the robot responds.

quiz.question: How does this five-stage pipeline relate to Module 1's sense-think-act loop?
options: It's an unrelated, completely new idea
It's the same loop, just expanded: map/localise are sensing, plan is thinking, drive is acting, and replan closes the loop again
It replaces the sense-think-act loop entirely
quiz.explain: Every stage maps back onto the original three-box loop — this lesson is that same idea, scaled up to its most capable form.
